Founder's Direct POV Document Status: V1 Product / Business Requirements.
Document niche: Apparel Niche.
AUTONOMOUS LISTING AGENT
V1 Business Requirements & End-to-End Listing Process is for Apparel / Fashion Marketplace Sellers.
Important Notice on Living Marketplace Rules
Marketplace schemas change.
The product must treat marketplace requirements as living rules rather than a one-time hard-coded field list.
Amazon explicitly provides marketplace/product-type schemas.
Amazon notes that requirements can change.
Flipkart states that listing rules are subject to change.
Marketplace required fields change.
Marketplace allowed values change.
Marketplace validation rules change.
Purpose of this Document
Document defines, in non-technical business language, exactly what the product must do when a seller wants to publish an apparel SKU across marketplaces.
Exactly what the product must collect, when a seller wants to publish an apparel SKU across marketplaces from one dashboard.
Exactly what the product must understand, when a seller wants to publish an apparel SKU across marketplaces from one dashboard.
Exactly what the product must create, when a seller wants to publish an apparel SKU across marketplaces from one dashboard.
Exactly what the product must validate, when a seller wants to publish an apparel SKU across marketplaces from one dashboard.
Exactly what the product must submit, when a seller wants to publish an apparel SKU across marketplaces from one dashboard.
Exactly what the product must monitor, when a seller wants to publish an apparel SKU across marketplaces from one dashboard.
Exactly what the product must repair, when a seller wants to publish an apparel SKU across marketplaces from one dashboard.
Exactly what the product must report, when a seller wants to publish an apparel SKU across marketplaces from one dashboard.
Seller publishes an apparel SKU across marketplaces from one dashboard.
Item | Definition
V1 product promise: seller gives basic brand + product information once.
V1 product promise: the agent turns it into marketplace-ready listings.
The agent manages the listing lifecycle until the listing is live or a human decision is genuinely required.
Primary niche: Apparel / fashion products.
Primary user: D2C brands managing apparel catalogs.
Primary user: manufacturers.
Primary user: traders.
Primary user: small sellers.
Primary user: marketplace agencies managing apparel catalogs.
Core outcome step 1: One product source of truth.
Core outcome step 2: → marketplace-specific listing.
Core outcome step 3: → validation.
Core outcome step 4: → submission.
Core outcome step 5: → error resolution.
Core outcome step 6: → live confirmation.
Operating principle: Do not ask the seller for information the system can reliably derive, reuse or validate.
Ask only when missing information materially blocks a correct listing.
1. Product in One Sentence
The Autonomous Listing Agent is a listing operations agent, not merely a content generator.
The agent takes a seller's product information and assets.
The agent builds a canonical product record.
The agent maps that product to each marketplace's category structure.
The agent maps that product to each marketplace's field structure.
The agent generates or transforms listing content.
The agent validates completeness.
The agent validates compliance.
The agent submits the listing.
The agent reads marketplace responses.
The agent fixes resolvable errors.
The agent asks the seller only for unresolved information.
The agent resubmits.
The agent confirms the final live status.
2. The End-to-End Flow
The complete lifecycle from seller onboarding to live verification consists of 19 operational stages.

Stage 1: capture stable legal identity once.
Stage 1: capture stable brand identity once.
Stage 1: capture stable tax identity once.
End-to-end flow stage 2 of 19: Marketplace account connection.
Stage 2: authenticate seller accounts.
Stage 2: store IDs.
Stage 2: store default commercial terms.
End-to-end flow stage 3 of 19: Product intake.

Stage 3: ingestion via CSV.
Stage 3: ingestion via ERP.

Stage 3: ingestion of size charts.
End-to-end flow stage 4 of 19: Product understanding.
Stage 4: isolate verified factual data from promotional marketing noise.
End-to-end flow stage 5 of 19: Category & sub-category classification.

End-to-end flow stage 6 of 19: Attribute extraction & normalization.

End-to-end flow stage 8 of 19: Marketplace schema mapping.

End-to-end flow stage 9 of 19: Content generation & optimization.
Stage 9: generate titles.
Stage 9: generate bullets.

End-to-end flow stage 10 of 19: Media and variant validation.

End-to-end flow stage 11 of 19: Compliance & completeness validation.

End-to-end flow stage 12 of 19: Human clarification only where necessary.
Stage 12: targeted single-question prompts for blocking gaps.
End-to-end flow stage 13 of 19: Marketplace submission.
Stage 13: dispatch validated payloads to marketplace APIs.
End-to-end flow stage 14 of 19: Submission/status monitoring.
Stage 14: asynchronous polling for feed outcomes.
Stage 14: webhook listeners for feed outcomes.
End-to-end flow stage 15 of 19: Error diagnosis.
Stage 15: translate raw portal error codes into plain actionable language.
End-to-end flow stage 16 of 19: Automatic correction.
Stage 16: auto-fix deterministic enum mismatches.
Stage 16: auto-fix formatting.

End-to-end flow stage 17 of 19: Resubmission.
Stage 17: safe bounded retry.

End-to-end flow stage 18 of 19: Live confirmation.
Stage 18: capture live URL.
Stage 18: capture marketplace SKU.

Stage 18: capture FSN (source: "ASIN/FSN").

Stage 19: show unified multi-marketplace operational view.
Stage 19: show audit trail.

4. Marketplace Strategy
V1 should be designed around a common apparel product model.
The common model is the source of truth.
Each marketplace adapter decides which fields are required.
Each marketplace adapter decides which fields are optional.
Each marketplace adapter decides which fields are conditionally required.
Each marketplace adapter decides allowed values.
Each marketplace adapter decides formatting rules.
Each marketplace adapter decides variation rules.
Each marketplace adapter decides submission/status behavior.
V1 should be designed around marketplace-specific adapters (plus the common apparel product model).
Target marketplace set can include Amazon.
Target marketplace set can include Flipkart.
Target marketplace set can include Myntra.
Target marketplace set can include AJIO.
Target marketplace set can include Meesho.
Target marketplace set can include Nykaa Fashion.
Target marketplace set is subject to the commercial/API access available to the business.
Category Semantic Variance: Do not assume that the same apparel category means the same thing on every marketplace.
No Hard-Coded Lists: Do not hard-code a single universal 'required fields' list.
Dynamic Schemas: for each connected marketplace, the product should maintain a current marketplace/category schema.
Dynamic Schemas: map the canonical product into each connected marketplace's current marketplace/category schema.
Amazon's developer documentation describes Product Type Definitions as the source for product-type and marketplace requirements.
Amazon Product Type Definitions include required/conditional attributes.
Flipkart's official Listing Management documentation separates product information from the seller listing.
Flipkart states that listing rules can change.
Because Flipkart listing rules can change, errors should be handled explicitly.

5.3 Seller Catalog Intake Options
The seller should be able to provide product information in multiple ways.
Intake option: Single product form.
Intake option: Bulk spreadsheet/template upload.
Intake option: Images + basic product information.
Intake option: Existing catalog export.
Intake option: ERP/PIM/catalog source, where available.
Intake option: URL/website product page, where permitted.
Intake option: Combination of the above.
Data Ingestion Rule
The system should merge these inputs rather than forcing the seller to repeat information.

7. Variants: The Product Family Model
The system must distinguish the product style from the sellable variant.
A common apparel family is one style with multiple colors and sizes.
Level | Example | Rule
Variant level 'Parent / style': example `TSHIRT-001`.
Variant level 'Parent / style' rule: Represents the underlying product/style.
Variant level 'Color child': example `TSHIRT-001-BLK`.
Variant level 'Color child' rule: One color variation.
Variant level 'Size child': example `TSHIRT-001-BLK-M`.
Variant level 'Size child' rule: One sellable size/color combination.
Variant level 'Marketplace listing': example Marketplace-specific SKU/listing ID.
Variant level 'Marketplace listing' rule: External representation of the sellable item.
Core Variation Invariants
Core Variation Invariant: store a complete size × color matrix.
Core Variation Invariant: the size × color matrix includes unavailable combinations.
Core Variation Invariant: never silently create a variant that the seller did not provide.
Core Variation Invariant: keep seller SKU stable even if marketplace identifiers differ.
Core Variation Invariant: record parent-child relationships separately from marketplace-specific variation rules.
Amazon's listing schema explicitly distinguishes parent and child listing levels.
Amazon parent and child listing levels have different attributes applicable to each.
8. Media / Image Intake
For apparel, image requirements can differ by marketplace.
Amazon's current seller guidance describes a main image for parent and child listings.
Amazon allows alternative images for details such as fabric, features and angles.
Media Field | What the Seller Should Provide | Agent Responsibility
Media field 'Main product image': seller provides Clean product image.
Agent responsibility for 'Main product image': Validate suitability.
Agent responsibility for 'Main product image': assign marketplace role.
Media field 'Additional images': seller provides Front/back/side/detail/lifestyle as available.
